lesson.title: Straight Up: Why Vertical Lines Have Undefined Slope
lesson.summary: An undefined slope happens when a line runs perfectly vertical, causing the slope formula's denominator to become zero, which division simply cannot handle.
lesson.body:
The slope formula, m equals (y2 minus y1) divided by (x2 minus x1), depends on dividing by the change in the x-coordinate. Division by 0 is not a valid operation in arithmetic. There is no number that, when multiplied by 0, gives back a nonzero result, so whenever the run in the denominator equals 0, the slope formula breaks down and the slope is said to be undefined, not 0 and not infinite, simply undefined.

This exact situation happens when a line is perfectly vertical. Every point on a vertical line shares the same x-coordinate, even though the y-coordinate is free to be anything. Since the x-coordinates of any two points on the line are identical, subtracting them in the slope formula always produces 0 in the denominator.

Check this with the points (3, 1) and (3, 8). Here x1 = 3, y1 = 1, x2 = 3, y2 = 8. Applying the formula gives m = (8 minus 1) divided by (3 minus 3), which is 7 divided by 0. The numerator, 7, is a perfectly fine nonzero number, but dividing it by 0 has no answer, so the slope is undefined. Plotting these two points shows why: both sit directly above and below each other at x = 3, with y ranging from 1 up to 8, tracing a straight vertical line with no horizontal movement at all.

It is worth contrasting undefined slope carefully with 0 slope, since students often mix them up. Zero slope comes from a 0 numerator over a nonzero denominator, describing a flat, horizontal line with no rise at all. Undefined slope comes from a nonzero numerator over a 0 denominator, describing a vertical line with no run at all. The two situations are opposites: one has all run and no rise, the other has all rise and no run. Neither one is bigger or smaller than the other in a numeric sense, because undefined slope is not a number on the number line to begin with, it simply falls outside what division can produce.

Undefined slope also explains a limitation of the slope-intercept and point-slope forms you will study soon, both of which rely on having a numeric slope to plug in. A vertical line cannot be written in either of those forms, because there is no value of m to use. Instead, a vertical line is written directly as x equals a constant, which you will look at closely as a vertical line. Whenever you compute a slope and land on a division by 0, that is not a mistake to fix, it is the algebra correctly telling you the line is vertical.

Try one more pair to reinforce the pattern: (negative 4, 0) and (negative 4, 9). Both points share the x-coordinate negative 4, so before even applying the formula you can predict the slope will be undefined. Confirm it: m equals (9 minus 0) divided by (negative 4 minus negative 4), which is 9 divided by 0, again undefined. A helpful way to remember the difference between 0 slope and undefined slope is to picture the two extremes of steepness. A perfectly flat road has 0 slope because it takes forever to gain any height at all. A sheer cliff face has undefined slope because it gains unlimited height while covering no horizontal distance whatsoever, which is exactly the situation the slope formula cannot express as a single number.
